steps.body: What if the top beats the bottom? **Keep jumping.** 5/4 means five jumps of a fourth: four jumps land you on 1, and the fifth carries you past it. The number line doesn't stop at 1 — and neither do fractions.

widget.prompt: This line runs 0→2, cut into fourths — 8 jumps in all. Slide to 5/4.
widget.lowFeedback: Not there yet — 5/4 needs five fourth-jumps, and the fourth one only reaches 1.
widget.highFeedback: Too far past — count back toward five jumps.
widget.successFeedback: Five fourth-jumps: one whole trip (4/4) plus one more jump. 5/4 lives between 1 and 2.

predict.prompt: This line runs 0→2. When you slide to 5/4, will you be before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1?
predict.reveal: Four fourth-jumps land exactly on 1 — the fifth jump steps beyond it. A fraction bigger than its bottom number lives past the whole.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents nl beyond one.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for nl beyond one must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines nl beyond one.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: Four fourths reach 1 and eight reach 2 — seven jumps stop one short of 2, so 7/4 sits between 1 and 2.
Split it: 7/4 = 4/4 + 3/4 = one whole and three-quarters more.

widget.prompt: Where does 7/4 live on the line?

options.label: Between 1 and 2
options.feedback: Past the first whole (4/4) but short of the second (8/4) — seven jumps land in between.

options.label: Between 0 and 1
options.feedback: The top (7) beats the bottom (4) — that means MORE than a whole trip. 7/4 has already crossed 1.

options.label: Exactly on 2
options.feedback: Exactly 2 would take eight fourth-jumps (8/4). Seven stops one jump shy.

options.label: At the number 7
options.feedback: The 7 counts JUMPS, not miles — seven quarter-jumps only carry you a bit past 1.

steps.body: Whole numbers wear fraction names on the line: **4/4 = 1, 8/4 = 2, 12/4 = 3**. Any n/n lands exactly on 1 — chapter 1's all-the-pieces, now a landing spot. A top bigger than the bottom just means more than one whole trip.

explanationVariants: Three third-jumps make each whole, so two wholes take 3 + 3 = 6 jumps: 6/3 = 2.
Count the whole-number landings: 3/3 is 1, 6/3 is 2 — every three jumps banks another whole.

widget.prompt: Jumping in THIRDS from 0, how many jumps land you exactly on 2?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 jumps is 2/3 — still inside the first trip. Reaching the number 2 takes two FULL trips of three jumps each.
3 jumps (3/3) lands exactly on 1 — the first whole. Keep going: three more reach 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Each whole costs 3 third-jumps — and 2 is two wholes out.

widget.prompt: Does each fraction land BEFORE 1, or ON-or-PAST 1?

items.feedback: Three of four jumps — one jump short of the finish.
Top beats bottom: the fifth jump crossed the line at 1.
Top EQUALS bottom — all six jumps taken, standing exactly ON 1.
Two of five jumps — still in the first half of the trip.

widget.missFeedback: Compare top to bottom: smaller top lands before 1; equal lands on it; bigger sails past.
widget.successFeedback: Top vs bottom tells the tale: 3/4 and 2/5 stop short; 6/6 stands on 1; 5/4 is past it.

explanationVariants: Nine jumps of a nine-cut trip is the complete trip — 9/9 stands exactly on 1.
Top equals bottom means every piece walked: the finish line itself.

options.label: Exactly on 1
options.feedback: All nine jumps of the nine-jump trip — the whole, standing on the 1 mark.

options.label: Just past 1
options.feedback: Past 1 needs a top BIGGER than the bottom (like 10/9). Equal top and bottom is exactly the whole.

options.label: Just before 1
options.feedback: Before 1 would leave a jump untaken (like 8/9). Nine of nine takes them all — landing on 1 itself.

options.label: At the number 9
options.feedback: Nine NINTH-jumps only cover one whole trip — 9/9 = 1, not 9.

hints: 3 jumps land on 1; 6 jumps land on 2.
The frog took 7 — one jump more than a landing you know.
explanationVariants: 6 jumps land exactly on 2, so the 7th puts the frog just past it — 7/3 sits between 2 and 3, and the smaller neighbor is 2.
Bank the wholes: 7/3 = 6/3 + 1/3 = 2 and one more third-jump.

widget.prompt: A frog jumps in THIRDS along the line, starting at 0. After 7 jumps it sits between two whole numbers. Enter the SMALLER of the two.

commonErrors.feedback: 3 is the neighbor on the FAR side — the frog would need 9 jumps (9/3) to reach it. It has only crossed 2.
7 counts the JUMPS, not the frog's position. Seven third-jumps only carry it a bit past the number 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Find the whole-number landings first: 3 jumps = 1, 6 jumps = 2 — then place jump number 7.

steps.body: The line is endless — so are fractions.
takeaways: Top bigger than bottom? Keep jumping past 1 — 5/4 is a whole plus a fourth.
n/n always lands exactly on 1; every b jumps banks another whole.
To place a big fraction, find the whole-number landings first, then count the extras.
steps.teaser: chapter 3: that strange moment when 2/4 landed on 1/2's spot — two names, one point.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Land on the whole numbers first: every b jumps is one whole — **b/b = 1, then 2b/b = 2**. Jumping in halves? 2 jumps = 1, 4 jumps = 2. Then count the leftover jumps past the last whole.

explanationVariants: Four half-jumps bank two wholes (4/2 = 2); the fifth adds one more half: 2 wholes and a half.
5/2 = 4/2 + 1/2 — two whole trips plus a single half-jump.

widget.prompt: A frog jumps in HALVES. After 5 jumps, where is it?

options.label: 2 wholes and one more half-jump
options.feedback: Four jumps bank 2 wholes; the fifth half-jump lands at 2½ — that's 5/2.

options.label: At the number 5
options.feedback: Five HALF-jumps cover half that distance — the frog sits at 2½, not 5.

options.label: Before 1
options.feedback: Just two half-jumps already reach 1 — five of them are well past it.
